discussion.q: Jesus says take the log out of your own eye first, then you will see clearly to help your brother with his speck. Where have you been quick to judge a fault in someone else that is larger and uglier in you?
discussion.behind: Move straight to self-implication, because the log is the point. We judge most fiercely the sins that mirror our own. The aim is honest recognition of a specific log we have ignored while inspecting others' specks. Go first, and keep it personal rather than abstract.

discussion.q: Jesus says keep asking, seeking, knocking, because the Father gives good gifts to those who ask. What does it change to know you come to a Father who wants to give, not a reluctant judge you have to wear down?
discussion.behind: Land the character of the One we ask. Many of us pray as though God needs persuading or is stingy with his children. The aim is to move prayer from wearing God down to trusting a Father who delights to give, which reframes both the asking and the waiting.

discussion.q: Jesus says the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and few find it, while the easy wide road that everyone travels leads to destruction. Why does the modern church find this so hard to say out loud?
discussion.behind: Press on the discomfort with the narrow gate. We prefer a wide, easy, agreeable Christianity. The aim is to name our resistance to the cost and exclusivity Jesus plainly states, and to ask honestly whether we have traded his narrow way for the broad road of a faith that demands nothing.

discussion.q: Bonhoeffer called the wide gate the way of cheap grace, a faith that costs nothing and so leads nowhere. Where in your own faith have you taken the wide, easy road and told yourself it was the way of Christ?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and Bonhoeffer. The wide road is comfortable and crowded, which is exactly its appeal. The aim is each person, the leader first, naming where they have chosen the easy version of following Jesus and called it the real thing. The point is honest reckoning, not despair.

objections.objection: Jesus clearly said do not judge. So who are Christians to tell anyone else how to live? Any time a believer calls something a sin, they are violating the plain command of Christ and being a hypocrite.
objections.response: This is the most popular misreading of the sermon, and Bell grants it nothing, because the text refuses it outright. Read just a few verses on, where Jesus tells the same hearers to watch out for false prophets, to know them by their fruits, not to give dogs what is holy. That is moral discernment, commanded in the very same breath. So do not judge cannot mean never assess right and wrong. What Jesus forbids is the hypocrite's judgment, the man with a plank in his own eye who appoints himself inspector of the specks in everyone else's, condemning in others what he excuses in himself. The command is not stop seeing clearly. It is the opposite. Take the log out of your own eye first, precisely so that you will see clearly enough to help your brother, gently, as a fellow patient and not as a judge on a bench. The verse does not abolish discernment. It demands humility before discernment.

objections.objection: The narrow gate and the few who find it sound cruel and exclusive. Why would a loving God make the way to life hard and the road to destruction the one most people are on? It feels designed to fail people.
objections.response: Hold the difficulty honestly rather than softening the words, because Jesus does say the gate is narrow and few find it, and pretending otherwise is no kindness. But notice what makes the gate narrow. It is narrow not because God is stingy with life but because the gate is a person, Christ himself, and there is no other way through, no wider entrance we get to invent. The wide road is wide because it asks nothing, costs nothing, and lets you carry everything, your self-rule, your idols, your refusal to be changed, all the way to the end. The narrow gate is narrow because you cannot bring those things through it. You enter empty-handed, as the very first beatitude said, poor in spirit. That is not cruelty. The God who set the narrow gate is the same God who came and stood in it himself and calls, with arms open, to everyone on the broad road, come this way, the hard way, the way that actually leads home.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the log in your own eye, the fault you have refused to look at in yourself while inspecting it relentlessly in others, that Jesus says you must remove before you can see at all?
sessions.practice: This week, do two things that the chapter holds together. First, take one person you have been quietly judging, name the speck you see in them, and then ask God to show you the log in your own eye that matches or exceeds it, and confess that first. Second, take one thing you have stopped asking God for because you assumed he would not give it, and begin asking again, daily, as a child asks a Father who gives good gifts. Write down what surfaced when you looked for your own log, and what changed when you started asking again.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have made do not judge into permission to excuse ourselves and a weapon to silence anyone who would correct us, and we have inspected the specks in everyone else while a log sat in our own eye. Forgive our hypocrisy. Teach us to take the log out first, to see clearly, to help gently. We have prayed as though you were reluctant, when you are a Father longing to give good gifts to your children. Teach us to keep asking. And we confess we have loved the wide, easy road and called it your way. Set our feet on the narrow path, the hard one, the one that leads to life, and keep us on it, because we cannot find it or hold it on our own. Amen.
reflection: What fault am I quick to condemn in others that lives larger in me, and why have I refused to take that log out first?
Do I pray as though God were a reluctant judge to be worn down, or a Father glad to give, and how would my asking change if I believed the second?
Where have I chosen the wide, easy road of a faith that costs me nothing, and what would the narrow gate actually require me to leave behind?
sessions.teaching: Matthew 7 reads like Jesus gathering up everything the sermon has scattered and pressing it into a handful of commands so plain they are impossible to misunderstand, which has never stopped us from misunderstanding them spectacularly. Judge not, that you be not judged. Ask, and it will be given to you. Enter by the narrow gate. The first question is how these even belong together, because at first they seem to pull against each other. The warning against judging sounds like it forbids drawing any moral line at all, and then the narrow gate seems to demand the hardest line imaginable. So let us take them in order, and let us start with the one the world has stolen. Judge not. This is, without much competition, the most quoted verse in the modern world, and it is almost always quoted to mean one thing. Never call anything wrong. It has become the favorite verse of a culture that wants its sins left strictly alone, the verse people who do not read the Bible somehow always know, deployed the instant anyone suggests that any behavior is anything other than fine. And Bell grants this reading nothing, because it is simply, textually false, and the proof is a few verses down the very same page. The same Jesus who says judge not, in the same breath, tells these same hearers to beware of false prophets, to recognize people by their fruits, not to throw what is holy to the dogs. You cannot watch out for a false prophet without judging that he is false. You cannot know a tree by its fruit without assessing the fruit. So whatever judge not means, it cannot mean never discern right from wrong, because Jesus commands moral discernment in the very same passage. What, then, does he forbid. Read the picture he draws, because it is unforgettable and a little absurd, which is the point. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye. Picture it. A man with an entire wooden beam protruding from his own eye, leaning in close, squinting, to extract a tiny splinter from someone else's. The thing Jesus forbids is not seeing clearly. It is the hypocrite's judgment, the self-appointed inspector who condemns in everyone else the very things he quietly excuses in himself, who has appointed himself to a bench he has no business occupying. And notice that Jesus does not end with leave the speck alone. He says, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. The goal is still to help the brother. But you cannot help anyone while a beam is blinding you, and the man who has honestly dealt with his own log comes to his brother's speck differently, gently, as a fellow patient who has been to the same surgeon, not as a judge passing sentence from above. The command does not abolish discernment. It demands humility as the price of admission to it. Then the asking, and the tone shifts entirely. Ask, and it will be given to you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened to you. And Jesus grounds it in the most ordinary picture of a father. Which one of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone. If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him. Hear the correction in that. We so easily pray as though God were reluctant, a stingy or distracted or irritated judge who must be worn down by our persistence, talked into giving what he would rather withhold. Jesus says no. You come to a Father, and not even a flawed human father hands his hungry child a rock. The asking is not wearing God down. It is a child trusting a Father who actually delights to give. And then, finally, the gate, and here Bell will not soften a single word, because softening it has become the great industry of the comfortable church. Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. We do not like this. We prefer a wide, agreeable, undemanding Christianity that asks little and offends no one, a faith with a gate so broad you barely notice passing through it. And Jesus describes exactly that broad road, and tells us where it goes. The wide gate is popular precisely because it is easy. It asks nothing. It lets you carry everything through, your self-rule and your idols and your settled refusal to be changed, the whole load, all the way to the end. The narrow gate is narrow because you cannot fit those things through it. You enter it the way the sermon began, poor in spirit, empty-handed, having left behind the very things the broad road let you keep. This is exactly what Bonhoeffer meant by the contrast between cheap grace and costly grace. Cheap grace, he wrote, is the wide gate, grace as a doctrine that forgives everything and requires nothing, that promises heaven without discipleship, the cross without the cross, a Christianity that costs the believer not one thing and therefore changes him not at all. Costly grace is the narrow gate, costly because it costs a man his life, and grace because it gives him the only life worth having. The wide gate, Bonhoeffer saw, leads nowhere good no matter how crowded it is, and the crowd is no comfort, because the question was never how many are on the road but where the road goes. And I have to walk myself up to this gate and tell the truth, because I have loved the wide road. I have wanted the grace that forgives without the grace that changes. I have judged specks with a log in my eye and called it standing for truth. I have prayed faithlessly, as though God begrudged me. And I have, more times than I want to admit, chosen the easy, agreeable, costless version of following Jesus and called it the real thing, because the broad road is comfortable and crowded and the narrow one is lonely and hard. The sermon will not let me stay there. It ends its body the way it began, with a choice that cannot be split down the middle. Two gates. Two roads. Two destinations. And a Lord who stood in the narrow gate himself, and from there, with his arms open, calls to all of us on the broad and crowded road. Come this way. It is harder. It is the only way that leads home.

scriptureStudy.note: Judge not, that you be not judged, for with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged. The warning is against the hypocrite's condemnation, not against all discernment, and it cuts by warning that the measure we use returns on us.

Why see the speck in your brother's eye and not the log in your own. First take the log out, then you will see clearly to help. The goal remains helping the brother, but only after honest dealing with one's own larger fault.

Do not give dogs what is holy, do not throw pearls before pigs. In the same passage that warns against judging, Jesus assumes real discernment, proving do not judge cannot mean refuse all moral assessment.
Ask and it will be given, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened. The persistence is not wearing God down but the steady trust of a child who keeps coming to a Father who gives.

If you who are evil give good gifts to your children, how much more your Father. The character of the One we ask is a generous Father, not a reluctant judge, which transforms both the asking and the waiting.

Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. The golden rule gathers the sermon's ethic into one positive command, an active love that does not wait to be deserved.

Enter by the narrow gate, for the way is hard that leads to life and few find it. Jesus refuses the wide, easy, crowded road, naming the cost of the way that actually leads home, the narrow gate Bonhoeffer called costly grace.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the theme of cheap grace against costly grace, because it is the lens through which Bonhoeffer read this entire sermon and the sharpest tool for examining our own discipleship. In the opening pages of Cost of Discipleship, written in 1937 against a German church drifting into accommodation with a murderous regime, Bonhoeffer defined cheap grace as the deadly enemy of the church, the grace we bestow on ourselves, the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance, baptism without church discipline, communion without confession, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ living and incarnate. Costly grace, he wrote, is the treasure hidden in the field for which a man sells all he has, the pearl of great price, costly because it costs a man his life, and grace because it gives him the only true life. A serious group should weigh Bonhoeffer's distinction against the whole sermon, asking where the wide gate of cheap grace has crept into a comfortable church that wants forgiveness without obedience and the cross as a symbol rather than a summons. Set it beside the consistent witness of the New Testament that faith and discipleship are not separable, that the same grace which justifies also transforms, and that a faith producing no fruit was never the saving kind. And weigh the cost Bonhoeffer himself paid, executed by the regime he resisted in the final weeks of the war, a man whose book on costly grace was not theory but his own road to a narrow gate. The discipline is to let the distinction examine us personally, to ask honestly whether we have chosen the costly grace that demands everything and gives everything, or the cheap grace of a wide road that asks nothing of us and so leads, however crowded, nowhere we want to arrive.

memoryVerse.text: Ask, and it will be given to you, seek, and you will find, knock, and it will be opened to you.

sessions.title: The House on the Rock
sessions.aim: To hear how Jesus ends the sermon, not with a summary but with a storm, dividing all his hearers into two builders, and to take seriously that the difference between the houses is not hearing but doing, and that the storm tells the truth.
sessions.summary: Jesus ends the greatest sermon ever preached with a story about two men building houses. Both hear the same words. Both build. The difference appears only when the storm comes, and then it is total, because one house stands and one falls with a great crash. The first question is what divides them, and Jesus states it plainly. It is not hearing his words. Both men heard. It is doing them. The one who hears and does built on rock. The one who hears and does not built on sand. Bell takes the strong form of the objection that this turns the gospel back into works, that we are saved by grace and not by doing, so the demand to do these words must be softened. He grants the truth in it, that we are saved by grace alone and could never earn the kingdom by our building. But he refuses the cheap conclusion, because Jesus is not describing how we earn salvation. He is describing what real faith looks like from the outside, and real faith does. A hearing that never becomes doing was never real hearing. Bonhoeffer said only the obedient believe, and only believers obey, that the two cannot be torn apart without killing both. And then the storm, which Bell will not let us avoid. The storm is not optional. It comes to both houses. It is not the storm that determines whether you stand, it is the foundation the storm reveals. The sermon does not end with a tidy application. It ends with a house standing in the rain and a house in ruins, and the quiet, weighty question of which one you have been building.

keyScripture.why: Jesus ends the sermon by dividing all his hearers into two builders whose houses look identical until the storm comes, and locating the whole difference not in hearing his words but in doing them, so that the foundation is revealed only under the flood.

discussion.q: Jesus ends the whole sermon with two builders whose houses look identical until the storm hits. Why do you think he ends with a storm instead of a summary or a tidy application?
discussion.behind: Open on the strangeness of the ending. We expect a conclusion, and Jesus gives a storm. The aim is to feel that the sermon does not resolve into advice but into a test, and that the storm is coming to everyone, which makes the foundation question urgent rather than abstract.

discussion.q: Both men heard the same words. The only difference was that one did them and one did not. Where have you been a hearer of the Sermon who has not become a doer of it?
discussion.behind: Move straight to self-implication, because hearing-without-doing is the whole danger. After five sessions of hearing, the question is what we have done. The aim is honest recognition of the gap between what we have heard in this study and how we are actually living. Go first.

discussion.q: Bell says a hearing that never becomes doing was never real hearing. Bonhoeffer said only the obedient believe and only believers obey. How does that challenge the way you have separated believing from doing?
discussion.behind: Press on the false split between faith and obedience. Many of us treat believing as the real thing and doing as optional extra credit. The aim is to feel that genuine faith necessarily acts, that a faith doing nothing was never the living kind, without sliding into salvation by works.

discussion.q: The storm comes to both houses. Jesus does not promise the faithful a life without storms, only a foundation that holds. How does it change things to know the storm is not optional, only the foundation is?
discussion.behind: Land the realism. The point is not avoiding storms but surviving them on the right foundation. The aim is to free the room from expecting that obedience buys an easy life, and to refocus them on what the storm reveals rather than on whether it comes.

discussion.q: Looking back over all six sessions, what is the one thing you have heard in this study that you most need to start doing, and what has kept you from doing it until now?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study with self-implication and a call to act. Do not resolve it neatly. Invite each person, the leader first, to name the specific obedience they have avoided and why. The point is to send the room out as doers, building on rock, not merely as hearers who enjoyed the sermon.

objections.objection: If the difference between the two houses is doing the words, then this whole sermon teaches salvation by works, which contradicts the gospel of grace. We are saved by faith, not by how well we obey the Sermon on the Mount.
objections.response: Bell grants the real concern, because it guards something precious, that we are saved by grace alone through faith and could never build our way into the kingdom by obedience. Hold that firmly. But notice what Jesus is and is not doing. He is not describing how a person earns salvation by the quality of his building. He is describing what living faith actually looks like when you watch it over time, and living faith does the words. The doing is not the root of salvation, it is the fruit of it, the visible evidence that the hearing was real. A faith that hears everything and does nothing is not a humble faith resting in grace, it is a dead faith, and James says exactly that, that faith without works is dead. Grace alone saves, and the grace that saves is never alone, it always produces a builder who builds. The two houses are not works against grace. They are living faith against an empty profession that only sounded like faith.

objections.objection: This ending is frightening, not comforting. If my house might be the one that falls, how can I ever have assurance? It sounds like I can never know whether I built on rock until the storm destroys me.
objections.response: Handle this gently, because the fear is real and the sermon does mean to sober us. But hear where the assurance actually lies, because it is not finally in the quality of your building. Remember how the sermon began. Blessed are the poor in spirit, the ones who know they have nothing to bring. The rock is not your performance, it is Christ himself, the words you are building on are his, and the assurance comes from being joined to him, not from grading your own house. You can examine your life honestly, not to torment yourself but to see whether your faith is the kind that does, and where you find it lacking, the answer is not despair but to come again, poor in spirit, to the One who is the foundation. The storm does not reveal whether you built well enough. It reveals whether you built on him. And he has never once let the house that rests on him fall.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If a storm came to your life tomorrow, the kind that strips away everything you have used to hold yourself up, what would it reveal about the foundation you have actually been building on all this time?
sessions.practice: This week, take the single most convicting thing from all six sessions, the one command of Jesus you have most clearly heard and most clearly not done, and do it. Not study it further, not admire it, not intend to. Do it, this week, in one concrete and costly act, however small. Then write down what it was like to move from hearing to doing, what resistance rose up, and what you learned about your own foundation in the doing that you could never have learned in the hearing.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you ended your sermon not with a summary but with a storm, and we have been hearers of your words who have not become doers of them. We have admired this sermon and not obeyed it. We have built houses that look fine in the sunshine and we are afraid of the rain. Forgive us. We cannot lay the foundation ourselves, because the rock is you, and the only thing we bring is the empty hands we came with. Make our hearing into doing. Build us on you, the only foundation that holds, and when the storm comes, and it will come, let it find us standing, not because we built well but because we built on you. Amen.
reflection: Over these six sessions, what have I heard clearly and not done, and what does that gap reveal about whether my hearing has been real?
Where am I trusting the appearance of my house, the way it looks in fair weather, rather than the foundation that only a storm would test?
If the rock is Christ and not my own building, what would it mean to come to him again, poor in spirit, and let him be the foundation I cannot lay myself?
sessions.teaching: We come to the end, and the end is not what we expect from a sermon, because Jesus does not conclude with a summary or a stirring call or a tidy application we can write in a margin and forget. He concludes with a storm. Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. Look closely at the two builders, because almost everything about them is identical, and that is the point. Both men build a house. Both presumably want it to stand. And both, Jesus says explicitly, hear these words of mine. The same words. This whole sermon, the Beatitudes and the deeper law and the love of enemies and the treasure and the narrow gate, both men have heard all of it. From the outside, in the dry season, the two houses may look exactly alike. You could not tell them apart by walking past. The difference is invisible, buried, down at the foundation where no one can see, and it stays invisible until one thing happens. The rain falls, and the floods come, and the winds blow and beat against that house. The storm is what makes the difference visible, and when it comes, the difference is not partial. One house stands. The other falls, and great was the fall of it. So the first question is what actually divides these two men, and Jesus does not leave us guessing, because he states it with perfect clarity, twice. It is not hearing his words. Both men heard. The wise man hears these words and does them. The foolish man hears these words and does not do them. The entire difference, the difference between a house that stands and a house that collapses into rubble, is the difference between hearing and doing. And this should land on us with real weight, because we have just spent six sessions hearing. We have heard about the poor in spirit and the deeper law and the love of enemies and the treasure of the heart and the narrow gate, and Jesus turns at the very end and says, the hearing was never the thing. The doing is the thing. Now take the objection seriously, because it is the right one and a good theologian will raise it immediately. If the houses are divided by doing, is Jesus not teaching salvation by works. Are we not saved by grace through faith, and not by how faithfully we obey this sermon. And we have to hold the truth in that objection with both hands, because it guards something precious. Yes, we are saved by grace alone. No one builds his way into the kingdom by the quality of his obedience. The very first beatitude already settled that, blessing the poor in spirit, the ones who come with nothing to bring. So Bell grants it fully. We are not earning the kingdom by our building. But then he refuses the cheap conclusion that some would draw from it, the conclusion that since we are saved by grace, the doing does not really matter and the demand to do these words can be quietly softened into optional advice. Because that is not what Jesus is doing here at all. He is not describing how a man earns his salvation by the excellence of his house. He is describing what real, living faith looks like when you watch it over time, and real faith does the words. The doing is not the root. It is the fruit. It is the visible evidence, revealed by the storm, that the hearing went all the way down into the foundation and was not just noise that passed through the ears on a pleasant afternoon. A hearing that never once becomes doing was never real hearing in the first place. This is exactly what Bonhoeffer fought for, against a church that wanted to separate believing from obeying so that it could keep the believing and skip the obeying. Only the obedient believe, he wrote, and only believers obey. He meant that you cannot tear faith and obedience apart without killing both, that a faith which produces no obedience is not a more spiritual or more grace-filled faith, it is a corpse, and an obedience that does not flow from faith is just dead works. The two are one living thing seen from two sides. The wise builder is not earning anything. He is simply a man whose faith was alive, and living faith builds, and so when the storm came, the life in his faith was revealed in a house that held. And then there is the storm itself, and Bell will not let us tiptoe past it, because we badly want to. Notice that the storm comes to both houses. Jesus does not say the wise man's house never sees rain. The rain falls and the floods come and the winds beat against both houses equally. The faithful are not promised a life without storms. That is not the promise, and it has never been the promise, and a Christianity that tells you obedience buys you a sunny life has sold you the wide gate. The storm is not optional. It is coming, to you, to your house, in some form and in some season, the loss or the grief or the failure or the death that beats against everything you have built. What is not fixed in advance is what the storm will find underneath. The storm does not determine whether you stand. It reveals what you were standing on the whole time. It is a truth-teller, the storm, exposing in an afternoon a foundation that was laid invisibly over years. And here, finally, is where I have to stand inside it, because this is the most exposing word in the whole sermon for a man like me, a man who has spent his life hearing these words and handling these words and preaching these words. I have built houses that look fine in the sunshine. I have admired this sermon from the pulpit and not done it in the kitchen. I have heard the command to love my enemy and nursed my grudge, heard the warning about treasure and clutched my security, heard the call to the narrow gate and strolled the wide one, and decorated the front of the house so beautifully that no one, sometimes not even me, could see there was sand underneath. And the rain is coming for my house too. So I will not end this study with a bow, because Jesus did not, and the bow would be a lie. I will end it where he ended it, with two houses, one standing in the rain and one in ruins, and a single quiet question that each of us has to carry out of this room and answer with our actual life. The foundation, remember, is not finally your performance. The rock is Christ himself, the words are his, the standing comes from being joined to him and not from grading your own walls. The poor in spirit, who came with empty hands, build on the only rock there is. So the question is not have you built well enough. The question is what have you been building on, and the only way you have ever found out, and the only way you ever will, is the storm. He has never once let the house that rests on him fall. Build there. And then, for the love of God and your own soul, do not just hear this. Do it.

scriptureStudy.note: You will recognize them by their fruits, a healthy tree bears good fruit. Just before the two houses, Jesus makes the same point about trees, the reality of a thing is shown by what it produces, not by what it claims.

Not everyone who says Lord, Lord will enter, but the one who does the will of my Father. Profession without obedience is not enough, and some who did mighty works in his name are unknown to him, sharpening that hearing and saying are not doing.

Everyone who hears these words and does them is like a wise man who built on the rock. The wise builder is marked by doing, and his house stands in the storm because of the foundation, not because the storm spared him.

Everyone who hears and does not do them is like a foolish man who built on sand, and great was the fall. The same hearing, the same storm, opposite ends, the whole difference is the doing that reaches the foundation.

The crowds were astonished, for he taught as one who had authority. The sermon ends with the authority of the teacher himself, the rock is not a principle but the person who spoke, whose words are the foundation.

Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. James draws out exactly the warning of the two houses, that hearing without doing is a self-deception, the man who looks in the mirror and forgets what he saw.

No one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Paul names the rock plainly, the foundation that holds is Christ himself, which is why assurance rests on him and not on the quality of our building.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the relationship between faith and works as the whole New Testament holds it, because the two houses sit precisely on the fault line where the church has so often stumbled, and a serious group should learn to walk it without falling off either side. On one side lies the legalism that reads the two builders as salvation by performance, as though the wise man earned his standing by the excellence of his obedience, a reading that crushes the conscience and contradicts the grace that saves apart from works. On the other side lies the antinomian error, the cheap grace Bonhoeffer named, that reads grace as making obedience optional, that hears the whole Sermon on the Mount and treats the doing of it as unnecessary because we are saved by faith alone. The historic Protestant formula threads the needle exactly, that we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone, it always and necessarily produces the fruit of obedience, so that works are not the root of salvation but its inevitable evidence. Read this alongside James, who insists that faith without works is dead, and Paul, who insists that salvation is by grace through faith and not of works, and see that they are not enemies but two witnesses to one truth, that living faith does. Set it against Bonhoeffer's claim that only the obedient believe and only believers obey, his refusal to let the church separate what God has joined. The discipline, and it is the discipline of the entire sermon, is to hold grace and obedience together so tightly that you can never use grace as an excuse not to obey, nor turn obedience into a way of earning the grace, but build, as a forgiven and empty-handed sinner, on the only rock there is, and do the words because you actually believe them.

memoryVerse.text: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock.

leaderPrimer: You did not have to do this, and the fact that you said yes matters more than you know. So before you open the first session, sit with me for a while, because this study will only go as deep as you are willing to go first, and the most important preparation is not mastering the material. It is letting the Sermon on the Mount get its hands on you before you hand it to anyone else. The aim of this series is narrow and it is heavy. It is to take the Sermon on the Mount at full weight, to keep Christ and his kingdom at the center of it, and to refuse two escapes at once, the one that turns the sermon into an impossible ideal so we are excused from doing it, and the one that turns it into a code we keep by trying harder so the gospel quietly becomes law again. Notice what the aim is not. It is not to make a roomful of people feel that they are failures because they cannot keep the sermon perfectly. It is not to produce a new legalism, a fresh list of rules to grade ourselves against. And it is not to soften the sermon into agreeable advice so that nobody leaves uncomfortable. If anyone leaves this series thinking the Sermon on the Mount is either hopeless or harmless, the study failed, however orthodox it sounded. Keep that in front of you. The single greatest danger you face as the leader of this particular study is the temptation to resolve the tension that Jesus deliberately leaves unresolved. The whole sermon lives in a held tension, grace and demand, gift and cost, the kingdom freely given to the poor in spirit and then the costly life that kingdom requires. You will feel a strong pull, every session, to collapse that tension in one direction or the other, either into a comfortable grace that lets everyone off the hook, or into a stern moralism that sends everyone home ashamed. Refuse both. The most important thing I can tell you, and I want to say it as plainly as I know how, is this. The Sermon on the Mount is grace before it is demand, and it is demand because it is grace. The kingdom is given to people with empty hands, who have nothing to bring, and that is the first beatitude and the foundation of everything. And then the same kingdom asks for everything, the anger surrendered, the enemy loved, the treasure relocated, the narrow gate entered, the words not merely heard but done. Hold both. The moment you let go of the grace, the sermon becomes a crushing law that produces either despair or hypocrisy. The moment you let go of the demand, it becomes the cheap grace Bonhoeffer warned about, a forgiveness that changes nothing and leads nowhere. Bonhoeffer is your companion through this whole study, so let me say a word about him. His Cost of Discipleship was written in 1937, in Germany, against a church that had made grace cheap and the demands of Jesus optional while the darkness gathered around it. He read this sermon not as an ideal to admire but as a call to follow, and he paid for that reading with his life, executed by the regime he resisted in the final weeks of the war. When you bring his voice into the room, bring the cost with it. He is not a quotable author. He is a witness who did the words. Now keep the room safe, because depth requires safety and this sermon goes after things people hide. It names anger and lust and the love of money and the grudges we nurse, the interior life we keep behind a clean surface. Any of it can surface, and when it does, the room must meet it with tenderness and not with shock or a quick fix. Safety here does not mean comfort. It means a person can admit the anger they have nursed, the lust they have hidden, the enemy they cannot forgive, the money they cannot release, without being lectured or recoiled from. Never let the group swarm a confession with advice. When someone is honest about a real struggle, slow the room down, thank them, and turn it back toward listening and prayer rather than solutions. You will face a few kinds of people, and you should know them before they arrive. The first is the perfectionist, who will hear the deeper law and the narrow gate and collapse into despair, certain they can never measure up. This person needs you to keep preaching the first beatitude back to them, that the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit, that the rock is Christ and not their performance. The second is the person who has quietly turned the faith into a comfortable, costless thing, the wide road, and who will resist the demand at every turn. This person needs the cost named gently but clearly, without contempt. The third is the wounded one, especially around the love of enemies and the refusal to retaliate, the person who has been told this command means they must stay and absorb abuse. Guard them fiercely. Say plainly, more than once, that loving an enemy means refusing personal vengeance, never submitting to ongoing harm, and that fleeing danger and seeking protection are not failures of this sermon. Now the part that matters most, the part it would be easiest to skip. Your own heart. You cannot lead people up a mountain you are not willing to climb yourself. If you walk in as the one who has the sermon figured out, dispensing its meaning to people who do not, you have already failed, because Bell does not stand on the mountain looking down and neither can you. He has nursed an anger he called principle. He has loved his money and called it stewardship. He has judged a speck with a log in his own eye, and chosen the wide road, and built houses that look fine in fair weather. He preaches this sermon as a man it convicts, and the power of this whole series depends on you doing the same. So before session one, let the sermon find you. Where is your anger, your money, your enemy, your wide road, your sand. Name it honestly, and do not hide it in the room. The leader who admits this sermon convicts me too can lead without contempt and without distance. The leader who pretends to have arrived will either crush the room by comparison or ring so false that no one trusts a word. One more practical word before the charge. Watch the clock and the weight together. These sessions go to exposing and costly places, and you are not aiming to leave people either crushed or let off the hook. When something heavy surfaces, do not rush past it and do not let the group fix it. Slow your own voice, thank the person, and when it is time, move the room toward the practice, the reflection, and the prayer, because none of this finally lands as an idea discussed. It lands as a life changed, as hearing that becomes doing. Trust the closing prayer and the practice to do work the discussion cannot. And resist with everything in you the urge to end each session, and especially the last, with a tidy resolution, because the sermon itself ends with a storm and a question, not a bow. The unresolved ending is not a failure. It is the truth, and it sends people out to do the words rather than merely to have enjoyed hearing them. Here is your charge. You are not the one who has mastered this sermon, and you are certainly not above the people you lead. You are a fellow builder who happens to be holding the readings, pointing everyone, yourself first, toward the King who preached it and then lived every word of it to a cross. Lead like that. Let the weight of these sessions rest on you first and most honestly. Refuse to crush the perfectionist and refuse to comfort the complacent. Keep grace and demand together in your own heart before you ask anyone else to. Guard the wounded. And when this sermon convicts you this week, say so out loud next session, because your honesty will preach louder than your competence ever could. The goal is not a room full of people who admire the Sermon on the Mount. The goal is a room full of people, you first, who have stopped merely hearing it and have begun, poor in spirit and joined to Christ the rock, to do it. Go honestly. Go costly. Go first.

faq.q: Is the Sermon on the Mount even possible to keep, or is it just an impossible ideal?
faq.a: This study refuses to answer that question with either of the easy escapes. It is not merely an impossible ideal that exists only to crush us and excuse us from doing it, because Jesus plainly expects his hearers to do what he says, to be salt and light now, and he ends the whole thing with a builder who hears the words and does them. And it is not a code we keep by trying harder, because the very first beatitude blesses the poor in spirit, the ones who have nothing to bring, which means the sermon is grace before it is demand. The honest answer is that the sermon is the shape of a life that has surrendered to the King, given to people with empty hands and then lived out by his power, not ours. You do not keep it by gritting your teeth, and you do not get excused from it because it is hard. You enter it poor, and you build on the rock, which is Christ himself.

faq.q: Does this study turn the gospel into a list of rules to follow?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent exactly that. Every session is anchored in the first beatitude, that the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit, the empty-handed, so the whole sermon rests on grace and not on performance. The study takes the strong form of the worry that the demands of Jesus become a new legalism, and refuses it, because the doing the sermon calls for is the fruit of living faith, not the root of salvation. The two houses at the end are not works against grace, they are living faith that does against an empty profession that only sounded like faith. The danger the study warns against is the opposite move too, the cheap grace that turns obedience into something optional. It holds grace and demand together, which is harder than either rule-keeping or letting ourselves off, and exactly what the sermon requires.

faq.q: Why does the study lean so heavily on Bonhoeffer?
faq.a: Because Bonhoeffer read this sermon the way it asks to be read, as a call to follow and not merely to admire, and because he paid for that reading with his life. His Cost of Discipleship was written in 1937 against a German church that had made grace cheap, a forgiveness that demanded nothing and changed no one, while a murderous regime rose around it. His distinction between cheap grace and costly grace is the sharpest tool the study has for examining our own discipleship, and his insistence that only the obedient believe and only believers obey holds together exactly what the sermon refuses to let us split. He is not quoted as a clever author but brought in as a witness, a man whose book on costly grace was not theory but his own road to a narrow gate, executed by the regime he resisted in the final weeks of the war.

faq.q: When Jesus says do not judge, does that mean Christians should never call anything wrong?
faq.a: No, and the study grants that popular reading nothing, because the text itself refuses it. A few verses after do not judge, in the same passage, Jesus tells the same hearers to watch out for false prophets, to know them by their fruits, not to give what is holy to dogs, all of which require moral discernment. So do not judge cannot mean never assess right and wrong. What Jesus forbids is the hypocrite's judgment, the man with a log in his own eye inspecting the speck in his brother's, condemning in others what he excuses in himself. The command is not stop seeing clearly. It is take the log out of your own eye first, precisely so you can see clearly enough to help your brother gently, as a fellow patient and not a judge on a bench. The verse demands humility before discernment, not the abolition of it.

faq.q: Does loving your enemies mean a victim has to stay and accept abuse?
faq.a: Absolutely not, and the study is careful to say so, because this command has been twisted to keep wounded people in harm's way and that is a sin the church must own. Loving an enemy means refusing personal retaliation, the private settling of scores, and wanting the other's actual good. It does not mean submitting to ongoing harm, and it never forbids fleeing danger or seeking protection or going to the proper authorities. A battered person escaping harm is not violating this command. Sometimes the most loving thing toward an abuser is to stop them, through lawful means, from continuing in their sin. The command kills your right to revenge. It does not kill your right to be safe. And the love Jesus asks for is a posture of the will that prays for an enemy and refuses vengeance, not a warm feeling you must manufacture toward someone who hurt you.

faq.q: Is the study saying I should not save money or plan for the future?
faq.a: No, and a careless reading of Matthew 6 lands there, but the reading is wrong. Scripture praises the ant who stores in summer and calls the man who will not provide for his household worse than an unbeliever. Jesus is not naming an amount and he is not forbidding prudence. He is naming a master. The question is not how much you have but what you are asking it to do. Money becomes a god the moment you trust it to do what only God can do, to secure your life, to prove your worth, to guarantee a tomorrow only God holds. You can save and plan and provide while your treasure is genuinely in heaven and your security genuinely in God, holding your money with an open hand as a tool rather than clutching it as a savior. The sin is not the savings account. It is the savings account doing the job of God in your heart.

faq.q: The narrow gate and the few who find it sound harsh. Why would a loving God make the way hard?
faq.a: The study holds the difficulty honestly rather than softening the words, because Jesus does say the gate is narrow and few find it. But notice what makes it narrow. It is narrow not because God is stingy with life but because the gate is a person, Christ himself, and there is no wider entrance we get to invent. The wide road is wide because it asks nothing and lets you carry everything through, your self-rule and your idols and your refusal to be changed, all the way to the end. The narrow gate is narrow because you cannot bring those things through it. You enter empty-handed, poor in spirit, as the first beatitude said. That is not cruelty. The God who set the narrow gate is the same God who stood in it himself and calls, with arms open, to everyone on the broad road, come this way, the hard way, the only way that leads home.

faq.q: What if I have heard all this before and nothing in my life actually changes?
faq.a: Then you are exactly the person the final session is about, and the study refuses to let that be comfortable. Jesus ends the sermon with two builders who both heard the same words, and the only difference between the house that stood and the house that fell was that one did the words and one did not. A hearing that never becomes doing was never real hearing. The study is built to push you from admiring the sermon to doing it, which is why every session ends with a concrete practice and the final session asks you to take the single most convicting thing you have heard and actually do it, this week, in one costly act. The point of the study is not a room of people who enjoyed the sermon. It is a room of people who began, poor in spirit and joined to Christ, to build on rock by doing the words.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is the Sermon on the Mount not just impossible moralizing that makes people feel guilty?
faq.a: It is a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn the right to answer it by refusing the cheap version of exactly that. It does not hand you a list of rules and tell you to feel bad for failing them. It begins by blessing the people who have nothing to bring, the poor in spirit, which is the opposite of moralism. It takes seriously how impossible the demands sound, the anger that is murder, the enemy you must love, and it locates the power for any of it not in your willpower but in a grace received first. The sermon is not finally a set of demands floating in the air. It is the description of a kingdom and an invitation from the King who preached it and then lived every word of it to a cross. You can weigh that. The study does not ask you to manufacture a guilt or a goodness you do not have. It asks you to consider the King.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer and the leader instead of just teaching the sermon?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the mercy. Bell does not stand on the mountain looking down as the man who has the sermon figured out. He has nursed an anger he called principle, loved his money and called it stewardship, judged a speck with a log in his own eye, walked the wide road, and built houses that look fine in fair weather. He preaches this sermon as a man it convicts, and the study asks every leader to do the same, because you cannot lead people up a mountain you refuse to climb. A leader who admits this sermon convicts me too can teach without contempt and without distance, as a fellow builder and not a judge. A study that pointed only at other people's sin would let everyone admire the sermon and do none of it, which is precisely the house built on sand.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have not figured out the Sermon on the Mount myself?
faq.a: You do not need to have figured it out. You need to be honest that you have not. The study is built to be led by a fellow builder, not by someone who has mastered the sermon and now dispenses it, and every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer and practice rather than advice, so you are not improvising. Your honesty about where this sermon convicts you, your own anger or money or grudge or wide road, may be the most pastoral thing in the room, the permission that lets others stop pretending. What you do need is to refuse two failures, crushing the perfectionist into despair and comforting the complacent into ease, to guard the wounded, and to point everyone, yourself first, toward the King who preached it and lived it. Read the leader primer, let the sermon find you, and trust the material.

faq.q: Does this study promise that if I obey the sermon my life will go well?
faq.a: No, and it deliberately refuses to. The sermon itself ends with a storm that comes to both houses, the wise builder's and the foolish builder's alike, which means obedience is not a purchase order for an easy life. The faithful are not promised a life without storms, only a foundation that holds when the storm comes, and a Christianity that tells you doing the words buys you sunshine has sold you the wide gate. The study ends without a tidy resolution, on purpose, with a house standing in the rain and a quiet question about what you have been building on. What it promises is not a smooth life but a rock that holds, Christ himself, and the assurance that the house resting on him has never once fallen, no matter how hard the rain. The point is not the absence of the storm. It is the foundation the storm reveals.

timeline.event: Moses receives the law on Mount Sinai, the mountain of the old covenant, and Matthew deliberately sets Jesus on a mountain to teach, presenting him as the new and greater Moses who does not abolish that law but brings it to its intended depth.

Jesus preaches the Sermon on the Mount to his disciples and the gathered crowds, opening with the Beatitudes and closing with the two builders, the most influential moral teaching in human history and the most quoted and least obeyed.
James, the brother of Jesus, writes that faith without works is dead and that we must be doers of the word and not hearers only, drawing out the very warning of the two houses for the early church.

Matthew gathers and arranges the sermon in chapters 5 through 7 of his Gospel, framing Jesus as the new Moses on the mountain and preserving the teaching for the church that would wrestle with it for two thousand years.

The early church, facing persecution under the Roman Empire, takes the love of enemies and the refusal to retaliate with great seriousness, and many Christians read the sermon as a call to nonviolence even under threat of death.

Augustine writes his commentary On the Sermon on the Mount, one of the earliest sustained treatments, reading it as the perfect pattern of the Christian life and wrestling with how its high demands relate to grace.

The radical Reformation and the early Anabaptists take the Sermon on the Mount as a literal rule of life, including the refusal to swear oaths and the renunciation of violence, and suffer severe persecution for their reading of it.

Martin Luther preaches and writes on the Sermon on the Mount, insisting against both the legalists and those who dismissed it that the sermon is for all Christians and must be held together with the gospel of grace, not turned into a new law for earning salvation.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer publishes The Cost of Discipleship, reading the Sermon on the Mount against a German church that had made grace cheap, and defining the difference between cheap grace, which forgives without changing, and costly grace, which costs a man his life and gives him the only life worth having.

Bonhoeffer is executed by the Nazi regime he had come to resist, in the final weeks of the war, a man whose writing on costly grace and the narrow way was not theory but his own road to a narrow gate.

Martyn Lloyd-Jones publishes his two-volume Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, a thorough evangelical exposition insisting the sermon describes the necessary character of every Christian and is not an optional ideal for the few.

John Stott publishes The Message of the Sermon on the Mount, titled Christian Counter-Culture, presenting the sermon as the description of a kingdom community whose values run deliberately against the surrounding world's.

Dallas Willard publishes The Divine Conspiracy, recovering the Sermon on the Mount as practical training in the kingdom of God available now, and rejecting the readings that file it away as an unreachable ideal.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for the courage it takes, because the Sermon on the Mount is the most admired and least obeyed teaching ever given, and we are about to stop admiring it from a distance and let it get close. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can be honest here about the anger you have nursed, the money you cannot release, the enemy you cannot forgive, the place your life does not match what you say you believe. Nobody is going to lecture you or recoil. Second, this study holds two things together that we usually pull apart. The sermon is grace before it is demand, the kingdom given to people with empty hands, and then it is demand because it is grace, asking for everything. We will not turn it into an impossible ideal we get excused from, and we will not turn it into a list of rules we keep by trying harder. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. This sermon convicts me too. I have nursed an anger I called principle. I have built houses that look fine in the sunshine. We are not standing on the mountain looking down. We are climbing it together. Tonight we are looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what Jesus actually says. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the week we are about to walk into, into the ordinary places where this either becomes something we do or stays something we only heard, because the whole sermon ends on exactly that difference.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, even though it is not all resolved, because Jesus ended his own sermon with a storm and a question and not with a tidy bow, and a tidy bow would be a lie. Take the weight of this toward Christ this week, and do not just carry it as an idea. Try the practice. Do the one thing you most clearly heard and have not done. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. The point was never to admire the sermon. It was to build on the rock by doing the words. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (9 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and the held tension of grace and demand, and walk session 1's opening questions slowly. Name that the sermon is grace before it is demand.
Week 2: Session 1, The Upside-Down Kingdom, full discussion and practice on the Beatitudes.
Week 3: Session 2, Salt, Light, and the Deeper Law, with extended time on the interior law reaching anger and lust.
Week 4: Session 3, Love Your Enemies, part one through nonretaliation and turning the cheek, with careful time for the wounded.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the love of enemies grounded in the Father and the cross, plus practice on praying for an enemy.
Week 6: Session 4, Where Your Treasure Is, the two masters and the worry that follows a divided heart.
Week 7: Session 5, The Narrow Gate, judging, asking, and the two ways, with Bonhoeffer on cheap and costly grace.
Week 8: Session 6, The House on the Rock, hearing and doing and the storm that reveals the foundation.
Week 9: Integration. Revisit all six practices, the scripture index, and the one thing each person most needs to do, with space to act on it.

cadences.name: The intensive (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the upside-down kingdom and the deeper law.
Week 2: Session 3, Love Your Enemies, with extended and careful time on nonretaliation and the cost.
Week 3: Session 4, Where Your Treasure Is, the two masters and the anxious divided heart.
Week 4: Session 5, The Narrow Gate, judging, asking, and the two ways.
Week 5: Session 6, The House on the Rock, plus a short integration close on doing the words and not merely hearing them.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: The central companion to this whole study, reading the Sermon on the Mount as a call to follow and not merely admire, and defining cheap grace against costly grace. Anchors every session and especially sessions 1, 5, and 6.

bibliography.title: The Divine Conspiracy: Rediscovering Our Hidden Life in God
bibliography.author: Dallas Willard
bibliography.note: Recovers the Sermon on the Mount as practical training in the kingdom available now, against the readings that file it away as an unreachable ideal. Useful across all six sessions.

bibliography.title: The Message of the Sermon on the Mount: Christian Counter-Culture
bibliography.author: John Stott
bibliography.note: A clear evangelical exposition presenting the sermon as the values of a kingdom community deliberately running against the surrounding world. Strong on sessions 1 and 2. Leader to confirm specific claims before attributing them to Bell.

bibliography.title: Studies in the Sermon on the Mount
bibliography.author: D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones
bibliography.note: A thorough two-volume exposition insisting the sermon describes the necessary character of every Christian and is not optional. Background across the study. Leader to confirm specifics before pressing them as settled.

bibliography.title: Matthew for Everyone, Part One
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: An accessible commentary setting the sermon within Jesus' announcement of the kingdom and the new exodus, helpful for the kingdom framing throughout. Leader to confirm before stating its arguments as the study's position.

bibliography.title: Sermon on the Mount, the Reformation Commentary tradition and Augustine's On the Sermon on the Mount
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: One of the earliest sustained treatments, reading the sermon as the pattern of the Christian life and wrestling with its demands and grace. Background for the going-deeper sections in sessions 1 and 6.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On the heart of Christ toward the weary and the empty-handed, useful for keeping grace at the center when the demands of the sermon press hardest. Supports sessions 1 and 6.

bibliography.title: The King Jesus Gospel
bibliography.author: Scot McKnight
bibliography.note: On the gospel as the announcement of Jesus as King and the kingdom he brings, helpful for hearing the Beatitudes as a kingdom proclamation and not a list of virtues. Background for session 1. Leader to confirm before attributing specific claims.

bibliography.title: Knowing God
bibliography.author: J. I. Packer
bibliography.note: On the character of God as Father, useful for sessions 4 and 5 where Jesus grounds both provision and prayer in a Father who knows our need and gives good gifts. Background, leader to confirm specifics.

bibliography.title: Studies on the love of God and the wrath of God
bibliography.author: D. A. Carson
bibliography.note: Helpful for holding the love and the justice of God together, which matters for the love of enemies in session 3 and the narrow gate in session 5. Offered as a balancing voice, leader to confirm before pressing as settled.

bibliography.title: The Imitation of Christ
bibliography.author: Thomas a Kempis
bibliography.note: The contemplative classic on following Christ in lowliness and surrender, a fitting companion to the costly discipleship the sermon describes. Background for sessions 1 and 6.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: On the restless heart that finds rest only in God, useful for the divided heart and misplaced treasure of session 4. Background, offered as a voice on the disordered loves the sermon reorders.

furtherReading: The Cost of Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for any reader who wants to sit longer with the costly grace and the call to follow that anchor this whole study.
The Divine Conspiracy, Dallas Willard, for those who want to recover the sermon as practical kingdom living available now rather than an unreachable ideal, leader to confirm specific claims.
The Message of the Sermon on the Mount, John Stott, for readers who want a clear, reliable exposition of the whole sermon as the counter-culture of the kingdom.
Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, Martyn Lloyd-Jones, for anyone who wants a thorough, searching, chapter-by-chapter treatment that refuses to let the sermon be optional.
Matthew for Everyone, N. T. Wright, for those who want to read the sermon within the larger story of Jesus announcing and embodying the kingdom of God.

glossary.definition: The opening blessings of the sermon, in Matthew 5, which announce the citizens of the kingdom as the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek, and the rest, describing not virtues we climb to but the shape of a life surrendered to a King who turns the world's order backward.

The first beatitude and the door into the whole sermon, the confession that you have nothing to bring to God, no rung to stand on, the spiritual bankruptcy that is the qualification for a kingdom given by grace and not earned by achievement.

The study's name for the order Jesus announces, in which the world's reckoning is reversed, the meek inherit the earth, the empty-handed are blessed, and the values that win the world's game are not the values that win the kingdom.

Jesus' relocation of the law from the outward act to the heart beneath it, naming anger as the root of murder and the lustful look as adultery already committed, so that righteousness is a matter of the interior life and not only the visible behavior.

Jesus' images for his people, in Matthew 5, both of which exist entirely for the sake of what surrounds them and cease to be themselves when turned inward, naming a faith whose whole point is its effect on the world.

The command, in Matthew 5, to refuse personal retaliation and to seek the good of those who hate you, grounded in the Father who sends sun and rain on the just and unjust, and possible only because Christ loved his enemies, us, to the cross.

The investment Jesus commends in Matthew 6, against treasure on earth that perishes, on the principle that where your treasure is your heart will follow, so that what we invest in is forming what we love.

Jesus' declaration that no one can serve God and money, that these are rival masters and the heart finally belongs to one, money becoming a god the moment it is trusted to secure, to prove worth, or to guarantee tomorrow, the jobs that belong to God alone.

The image, in Matthew 7, of the hard way that leads to life and is found by few, against the wide easy road that many travel to destruction, narrow because the gate is Christ himself and you cannot carry your idols through it.

The closing parable of the sermon, two builders whose houses look identical until the storm reveals the foundation, dividing all hearers not by whether they heard the words but by whether they did them.

Bonhoeffer's term for grace as a doctrine that forgives without requiring repentance and promises heaven without discipleship, the wide gate, a forgiveness that costs nothing and so changes nothing and leads nowhere good.

Bonhoeffer's term for the grace of the narrow gate, costly because it costs a man his life and grace because it gives him the only life worth having, the treasure in the field and the pearl of great price for which one sells all he has.

Jesus' image, in Matthew 7, of the hypocrite who inspects the speck in his brother's eye with a log in his own, naming the self-excusing judgment Jesus forbids, and the command to remove the log first so as to see clearly enough to help.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The Sermon on the Mount is the most admired and least obeyed teaching ever given, quoted by people who would never live it and softened by a church that prefers it harmless. This six-session study, in the voice of James Bell and leaning on Bonhoeffer's Cost of Discipleship, walks slowly through Matthew 5 through 7, the upside-down kingdom of the Beatitudes, the deeper law that reaches anger and lust, the love of enemies, treasure and worry, the narrow gate, and the two houses in the storm. It refuses to make the sermon an impossible ideal or a list of rules, and it ends not with a tidy bow but with a question about what you have been building on. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Come to do the words, not just hear them.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We are starting a six-week study on the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5 through 7, leaning on Bonhoeffer's Cost of Discipleship, and before anyone braces for either a guilt trip or a greeting card, hear this. We are going to take the sermon at full weight, grace before it is demand and demand because it is grace, and we are going to stop admiring it from a distance and ask what it would mean to do it. It implicates the preacher first, because this sermon convicts me too. No homework, and no prep needed to lead a group. If you have ever wondered what Jesus actually meant on that mountain, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Jesus opened the greatest sermon ever preached by blessing the people the world had written off, and ended it with a storm. A six-session study on the Sermon on the Mount, in the voice of James Bell and leaning on Bonhoeffer, on the upside-down kingdom, the deeper law, the love of enemies, treasure and worry, the narrow gate, and the house that holds in the storm. It refuses to make the sermon harmless. Come to do the words, not just hear them.
quoteCards: The first qualification for the kingdom is the confession that you have no qualification. Blessed are the poor in spirit.
Jesus did not lower the law. He drove it inward, past the hand to the heart, where you actually live.
We love our enemies because we were the enemies, and were loved first.
Money becomes a god the moment you ask it to do what only God can do, to secure you, to prove your worth, to promise you tomorrow.
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The treasure leads. The heart follows it home.
The wide gate is crowded because it costs nothing and lets you carry everything through. The narrow gate asks for your hands to be empty.
The storm comes to both houses. It does not decide whether you stand. It reveals what you were standing on.
A hearing that never becomes doing was never real hearing. Do not just admire this sermon. Do it.
